title: "About eco"
---

```{r}
#| label: stats
#| include: false
s <- jsonlite::read_json("data/site_stats.json")
```

**eco** is a collection of ecological detection data in one format. Its
`r s$n_tables` tables come from `r s$n_deposits` public deposits (occupancy
surveys, repeated counts, capture histories, community surveys, eDNA). Each
table is one survey design from one deposit, converted to a single long table
with the same core columns, a species list resolved against GBIF, and metadata
that says how the survey was run and what was left out. The tables are versioned on Redivis and readable from R without an
account.

It is for anyone who wants many real surveys rather than one: to see how a
method behaves across designs and taxa, to compare models on data they did
not simulate, or to find a survey with a particular structure without
reformatting it first. The [glossary](glossary.html) says what eco means by
table, deposit, unit, period and the other words used here.

## Where it came from

eco is an offshoot of the
[Item Response Warehouse](https://itemresponsewarehouse.org), which does the
same thing for item response data in psychology and education: one long
table per dataset, so methods can be tested on hundreds of real datasets at
once. Occupancy and capture-recapture data share that structure, a unit with
a latent state observed imperfectly over repeated probes, and eco asks
whether the same approach serves ecology.

## How the tables are made

Every table is built by one R script in the repository's
[`data/`](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/tree/main/data) directory. The
script downloads the deposit, reshapes it, asserts facts about the source so
that a changed deposit fails loudly, and states in its header the source,
licence, mapping and what was not shipped. Every table must pass a validator
that cites the [standard](standard.html)'s clauses before it is released.

The scripts, the validator and most of this site were written largely by
Claude (Anthropic), an AI coding agent, working from a written
[processing guide](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/blob/main/processing_guide.md)
and reviewed by a psychometrician who is new to ecology. Each release is
published by hand. The scripts are short and public: if you rely on a table,
read the one that built it, and if a table is wrong, say so in an
[issue](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/issues).
[Releases and corrections](corrections.html) says what happens next.

## What is on this site

- **Data**: [every table](data.html) with its design, size, source and
  licence; [notes](data_notes.html) a user should read before fitting a
  model; and the [release history](corrections.html).
- **Use it**: the [R package](r.html) that reads tables and reshapes them
  for `unmarked`, `marked` and the AHM code, and [worked vignettes](vignettes/index.html).
- **The format**: [the standard](standard.html), the
  [design decisions](design.html) behind it, how to
  [convert a deposit](contribute.html), and a [glossary](glossary.html).

## Citing and licences

Each table keeps the licence of its source, shown on its entry on the
[Data](data.html) page; most are CC0 or CC BY. Every table is someone's
fieldwork: cite the original deposit and paper for each table you use, not
only eco, and the eco version you read, which pins the data (`eco_version()`).
`eco_cite()` in the [R package](r.html#how-to-cite) writes the reference list
or BibTeX for the tables you used, one entry per deposit. What else we ask of
users, on licences, commercial use and coarsened coordinates, is in
[Using eco responsibly](use.html).
